newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company -- CLARKE SHOWS CAUTION ON TAX CUTS

The chancellor Kenneth Clarke has announced a reduction of 1p in the pound in the basic rate of income tax. The reduction in tax was the smallest pre-election cut introduced by the Conservatives since 1979. The cut shaved public revenues by 2.2 billion stg, although most of this will be recouped through increases in indirect taxes and the closing off certain taxation loopholes. Looking to the prospects for the British economy, the chancellor noted that consumer spending would continue to provide the impetus for growth in 1997. In reaction, the markets have noted that Clarke may not have accomplished enough to avoid having to increase interest rates over the coming months.
-- POLICE TO PROBE LEAK OF DETAILS TO MIRROR

The police have been called in to investigate the leaking of details of the Budget to the Mirror newspaper. The government has warned that it is taking the disclosure extremely seriously and that the culprit, if caught, will face severe disciplinary action. Although the Mirror did not publish the leaked data, claiming it would be against the public interest, it has emerged that it had initially intended to do so but backed away for fear of being the victim of an elaborate hoax.
-- BLAIR DESCRIBES THE BUDGET AS TORY 'OLD CON TRICKS'

The leader of the Labour party, Tony Blair, in reaction to the latest Conservative Budget, has accused the chancellor of giving with one hand and taking away with the other. He also noted that in the wake of the latest package, the average family stood over 2,000 stg worse off today than they were in 1992. Meanwhile, shadow chancellor Gordon Brown has noted that, in the light of this Budget, Labour will probably make clear in January its own spending plans should it win the next general election.
-- CORPORATE TAX LOOPHOLES TO BE SCRUTINISED

As part of a wider drive to increase corporate tax revenues, several multinational companies that currently pay little tax in Britain will come under closer scrutiny, particularly with regard to the use of tax loopholes by their legal corporate tax-planning strategies. Meanwhile, in what some have described as a "disguised windfall tax", the privatized utilities are expected to be affected by plans to reduce the annual rate of capital allowances on plant and machinery.
-- DISTILLERS PRAISE 4 PERCENT CUT IN SPIRIT DUTY

Distillers have welcomed the decision to reduce by 4 percent the duty imposed on spirits. The move will reduce the price of a bottle of whiskey by 26p and will cut the difference in prices for spirits in the UK and on mainland Europe. The reduction was not, however, matched in the spirits and wine sector, where duty was frozen, disappointing brewers who warned that it will lead to job cuts in an industry being hard pressed by cheap imports from Europe. Cigarettes will increase by 15p per packet of 20.
-- DEARER MOTOR, HOME AND CONTENTS COVER

The cost of insurance for motor vehicles and home contents is set to rise next April as a result of the decision by the chancellor to increase the tax on premiums from 2.5 percent to 4 percent. Some insurance companies had, however, expected the rise to be much steeper, though there was a reaction of general disappointment from the industry to the news. The Association of British Insurers described the tax as a regressive one that affected the prudent most severely. Increases in costs are expected to be passed on to the consumer.
-- LAMENT AS LAST ORDERS ARE CALLED ON POPULAR SCHEME

Tax relief on profit-related pay is to be phased out between 1998 and just after the turn of the century, a move that is expected to save the treasury some 3.1 billion stg a year. Introduced 10 years ago, the scheme had grown in popularity and cost to the government. Chancellor Kenneth Clarke said the scheme could no longer be justified to the 22 million workers who were not part of it yet were effectively subsidising it.
-- NHS RECEIVES 1.6 BILLION STG FUNDING BOOST

The National Health Service has secured another 1.6 billion stg in public spending for 1997. In real terms, spending rises by 2.9 percent to 33 billion stg. An expansion in the Private Finance Initiative, aimed at involving the private sector in the construction of hospitals, was announced. Also, an additional 830 million stg is to be allocated to schools and universities next year. The private finance sector is to be sold accumulated student debts, expected to be worth some 3 billion stg over the next three years.
-- UNITED DRUG ADVANCES AND SEEKS I12.4M

Irish pharmaceutical, medical and consumer goods group United Drug has reported a 19 percent increase in pre-tax profit for the year to September, to 6m Irish pounds. United, which has invested 23m Irish pounds in infrastructure and acquisitions in the Republic and Northern Ireland over the past 10 years, announced a 12.4m Irish pounds rights issue, to allow for further possible acquisitions and strengthen its balance sheet.
-- ENERGIS ON COURSE TO BREAK EVEN

Energis, the telecommunications subsidiary of electricity distributor National Grid, has reported a 24 percent reduction in first-half operating losses to 30.3m stg. However, following strong growth and increased orders, the company said it is on course to break even on an Ebitda (Earnings before interest, tax and depreciation) basis next year. Energis, which now routes more than 60 percent of all the UK's Internet traffic, currently handles 3m calls a day on its network and has secured several large business contracts over the past six months with companies such as British Gas, ICL and Swinton Insurance.
-- NATIONAL GRID FORECASTS 4 PERCENT RISE IN DIVIDENDS

Electricity distributor National Grid has forecast real dividend increases of between four and five percent over the next four years. The company plans to attain this growth via a six percent (real) a year reduction in controllable costs. The costs reduction forecast is much greater than what the firm said it could meet when it underwent a regulatory review with Stephen Littlechild of Offer. In the meeting, which formed the basis of the regulator's price controls announced last month, National Grid said it could not meet cost cutting targets above two percent without damaging long-term profitability.
